title: Laborem Exercens (1981)
hook: John Paul II: work is for the person, not the person for work

segments.voice: Yesterday, Justice in the World: acting for justice is part of preaching the gospel, starting at home. Your line was justice is gospel. Did your one just act get done? Day one thousand three hundred seven.

A field of grain on a sabbath. Jesus's disciples are hungry, and as they walk they pluck the heads of grain. Critics object: that's work, and it's the day of rest. In Mark's Gospel, Jesus answers with a sentence that flips the order around. In the Douay-Rheims: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." The rule serves the person. Not the other way round. This path met the heart of John Paul the Second's letter on human work with the carpenter of Nazareth. Today, the rest of that letter, Laborem Exercens, which makes the same flip about the job you go to on Monday. Work is for the person, not the person for work. Today's word.
screen: `GRAIN ON THE SABBATH.` → `MADE FOR MAN.` → `WORK FOR THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: First, people before capital. Laborem Exercens says work has priority over capital. Capital here means the money, machines, buildings and tools of a business. The letter's point is that all of these are things, and things are meant to serve persons. It adds a twist: the machines themselves are the fruit of earlier human work, the inheritance of generations of workers. Capital is work, piled up. So it makes no sense to let the pile rule the people. Second, the boss behind the boss. John Paul the Second distinguishes a direct employer, the one who signs your contract, from what he calls an indirect employer: the laws, governments, markets and international arrangements that shape what any direct employer can offer. Whether work treats people well depends on that whole web, not just on whether your manager is kind. Third, the tiredness. The letter doesn't pretend work is always joyful. It's honest about sweat and toil. And it offers Christians a way to carry that: work as a share in God's activity as creator, and its hardness, borne patiently, as a share in Christ's cross. Not a reason to accept unjust conditions. A way to find meaning inside honest, hard days. Fourth, Monday. If work is for the person, then a person crushed by work has the order upside down, like a sabbath that starves the hungry. The person comes first: before the target, before the inbox, before the machine.
screen: `PEOPLE BEFORE CAPITAL.` · `THE BOSS BEHIND THE BOSS.` · `SWEAT, CREATION AND THE CROSS.` · then, large: `THE SABBATH WAS MADE FOR MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest from overwork. For these two minutes, no task, no list, no planning tomorrow. Settle, and breathe. Notice where work lives in your body: the jaw, the shoulders, the eyes, the hands. Let each one go a little, in turn. If thoughts of what's undone arrive, let them stand outside the door. They'll be there later. You are not a machine on pause. You are a person resting. If you pray, you can rest before God the way the sabbath invites. If you don't, simply rest. The bell holds the time.
Laborem Exercens. John Paul the Second's letter on human work: people before capital, a whole web of employers, and work made for the person. Today's word.
Your line: the person first. Today, set one boundary on work: a real lunch, a phone left in a drawer, or a stopping time you keep. Day one thousand three hundred seven.

howItsDone: Catholics often draw on Laborem Exercens in labor ministry, in Catholic business ethics and in keeping Sunday as a day of rest, and the letter is a standard text in Catholic teaching on work.

fork.setup: you run a workshop. new machines could make more if your people worked longer, faster, with fewer breaks. what does Laborem Exercens put first?
options: the machines: they cost the most.
the output: work is measured by what it makes.
the people: work is for the person.
fork.reveal: the letter gives work priority over capital. the machines are themselves the fruit of earlier work, and things exist to serve persons.

original.note: Latin: doing work, or exercising labor, the letter's opening words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Latin title about labor.
what it means: a letter saying work is for the person, not the person for work.
what a scholar hears: the priority of labor over capital, and the indirect employer.

notes: Day 1297 (the dignity of work) already uses Mark 6:3, Genesis 2:15, the subject-of-work point and sabbath rest; this day takes the priority of labor over capital, the indirect employer, and toil and the cross instead.
§12 paraphrase: capital as the fruit of the work of earlier generations; confirm.
§17 paraphrase of the indirect employer (state, laws, international structures); confirm.
§27 paraphrase: toil united to Christ's cross; §25 work as sharing in the Creator's activity. Confirm.
Original note: 'laborem exercens' rendered loosely; confirm the gloss and church-Latin pronunciation.
Editor pass: acknowledged that day 1297 already gave Laborem Exercens' central idea, so today reads as the rest of the letter.
